claims.text: In situ aberration-corrected STEM heating combined with molecular dynamics simulations can be used to investigate the atomic-scale thermal response of high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles exhibit a size-dependent thermal response.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles begin surface atomic diffusion at lower temperatures than larger particles.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles undergo more pronounced phase segregation than larger particles at elevated temperatures.
The initial FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles are nearly equiatomic.
The initial FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles are homogeneous and single-phase.
The nanoparticles span approximately 5–50 nm in size.
Real-time STEM imaging can monitor thermally induced atomic structural evolution while molecular dynamics provides complementary atomistic simulations.
The thermal response can be investigated over a temperature interval from approximately 298 K to 973 K.
The proposed STEM heating is conducted under high-vacuum, controlled-atmosphere conditions.
Elevated-temperature FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles develop pronounced atomic diffusion.
Phase-segregated layers form preferentially at the nanoparticle surface during heating.
Increasing temperature enhances atomic diffusion and drives progressive surface phase segregation.
Smaller nanoparticles have a higher surface-to-volume ratio than larger nanoparticles.
The higher surface-to-volume ratio of smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles causes more pronounced surface restructuring and phase separation.
Larger FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles remain compositionally and structurally uniform up to higher temperatures than smaller particles.
At room temperature without thermal treatment, FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles remain homogeneous and single-phase without significant surface segregation.
